subject: Endpoint tail behavior synthesis and multi-tenant SLO derivation
messages:
From: Tessa Morgan <tessa.morgan@redwood.com>
To: Anjali Rao <anjali@oriondata.com>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>, Diego Fernandez <diego.fernandez@redwood.com>
Date: 2025-06-12T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Endpoint tail behavior synthesis and multi-tenant SLO derivation

Hi Anjali —

Thanks again for sharing Orion's RFP. Per section 4 (performance validation) we put together a short benchmark spec that maps to the items you asked for: latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99/p999), throughput curves, cold-start/cold-cache behavior, and multi-tenant isolation evidence. I've attached redwood_benchmark_spec.md for your review.

Quick ask from our side to make the run deterministic and comparable across vendors:
- Please confirm the expected tenant mix (attach traffic mix CSV if available).
- Target SLOs you want expressed per-tenant (p95/p99) and any penalties tied to percentiles.
- Whether replay of production traces is preferred vs. synthetic synthesis (we support both; replay is best for cache effects).
- Any model variants to pin (e.g., quantized vv full-precision) and token length distributions.

Highlights from our recommended test methodology (short):
- Warmup: 30–60 minutes at nominal load to stabilize KV/prefix cache.
- Ramp/soak: step-ramp to 1x/2x/3x expected peaks with 10–30 minute soaks at each step.
- Spike tests: short 1–2 minute bursts at 5x to validate graceful degradation/fallback.
- Measurement: sample at 1s resolution, export per-replica percentiles; correlate with cache-hit metrics.
- Control plane: pin model version and GPU affinity for the duration; capture system metrics (GPU, host CPU, NIC stats).

On multi-tenant SLO derivation specifically: we typically produce a workbook that walks from raw latency samples -> per-tenant contribution -> derived SLO (we include headroom factors and variability bands). If you can share the tenant mix and the target percentiles, we'll pre-populate that workbook.

Proposed next step: if you can send the traffic mix and any contractual SLO targets by EOD Wednesday, we'll produce a candidate test plan and an exemplar SLO derivation workbook. If helpful, we can book a 60-minute technical runbook review.

Thanks —
Tessa Morgan
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

redwood.com

From: Anjali Rao <anjali@oriondata.com>

Subject: Re: Endpoint tail behavior synthesis and multi-tenant SLO derivation

Tessa —

Appreciate the spec. Attaching our current traffic mix snapshot (orion_traffic_mix.csv). Key points:
- Tenants: ~120 active; traffic distribution roughly: 70% low-throughput (chatty, short prompts), 20% medium (batch-ish embeddings/qa), 10% high-throughput (large-batch generation).
- Token lengths: median 22 tokens, 95th pct ~180 tokens.
- Expected concurrency: 350 steady-state, peak bursts up to ~1,200 concurrent across the fleet.
- We anticipate pinning to the quantized model variant for production tests.

Question: for multi-tenant SLO derivation, do you provide both a per-tenant guarantee and an aggregate SLA? Our procurement team prefers a mapping: per-tenant SLOs for top-20 tenants and an aggregate p95/p99 for the platform. Please include an exemplar deliverable in the workbook.

Also, please confirm whether Redwood will include evidence of graceful degradation (fallback to smaller model or queue behavior) during spikes — that's a requirement for our legal team.

Thanks,
Anjali Rao
Head of Vendor Evaluation, Orion Data
procurement@oriondata.com

Attachment: orion_traffic_mix.csv

From: Tessa Morgan <tessa.morgan@redwood.com>
To: Anjali Rao <anjali@oriondata.com>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>, Diego Fernandez <diego.fernandez@redwood.com>
Date: 2025-06-14T08:25:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Endpoint tail behavior synthesis and multi-tenant SLO derivation

Anjali —

Thanks for the traffic snapshot, that's perfect. We've pre-filled a "slo-derivation-workbook.xlsx" and attached an infra diagram to show how we isolate tenants at the serving layer. High-level responses to your asks below, plus the workbook includes worked examples for the top-20 tenants per your request.

1) Per-tenant vs aggregate SLOs (approach):
- We compute an empirical per-tenant percentile from an isolated replay (preferred) or a tenant-weighted sample from mixed runs.
- Aggregate platform SLO = weighted percentile across tenants where weights = tenant qps share. For example, if tenant A contributes 40% of qps, its p95 samples dominate the weighted p95.
- We publish both: per-tenant p95/p99 for the top-20 and an aggregate p95/p99 for billing/SLA.

2) Example derivation (from workbook):
- Baseline (single-tenant, warm cache) observed: p95 = 120ms, p99 = 420ms.
- With mixed tenancy and realistic cache interactions, weighted aggregate p95 observed = 160ms, p99 = 630ms.
- We apply a headroom factor (configurable, default 1.2) to map observed percentiles to contractual SLOs to allow for day-to-day variance.
- So derived contractual SLO (aggregate p95) = observed_aggregate_p95 * headroom_factor = 160ms * 1.2 = 192ms.

3) Accounting for cache/quantization effects:
- We log per-request cache hit/miss tags and compute 'effective token-time' conditional on hit-rate. The workbook gives a step-by-step calculator: effective_latency = measured_latency / (1 - miss_rate_adjustment).

4) Test matrix we propose (included in workbook):
- Replay: per-tenant replay for top-20 (captures prefix/KV cache realistic behavior).
- Synthetic step-ramp: 0.5x -> 1x -> 2x -> 3x nominal with 20 min soaks.
- Spike soak: 5x short bursts (90–120s) to validate fallback.
- Saturation curve: linear increase in QPS until error rate jumps; record per-token CPU/GPU efficiency.

5) Graceful degradation evidence: yes — we will demonstrate fallback flows (smaller quantized model, degraded output cadence, controlled queuing) and include time-ordered recordings of request-level fallback events with timestamps.

Operational notes:
- We will pin model_version=redwood-quant-v2 and apply identical quantization across replicas.
- For multi-tenant runs we use tenant-label-aware routing so we can slice results by tenant during analysis.
- Recommended sampling: compute p95/p99 on both request-latency and per-token-latency; include p999 for tail safety.

Next steps: we've attached slo-derivation-workbook.xlsx (pre-populated with your supplied mix) and infrastructure-diagram.pdf. If that looks good, I'll book a 60-minute runbook review (calendar link below) and propose to run a quick 3-hour pilot test next week to generate baseline evidence.

Link: https://calendar.redwood.com/meetings/9f3a6b-slo-sync

Regards,
Tessa Morgan
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
T: +1 415 555 0192

Attachments: slo-derivation-workbook.xlsx, infrastructure-diagram.pdf

From: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>
To: Tessa Morgan <tessa.morgan@redwood.com>, Diego Fernandez <diego.fernandez@redwood.com>
Date: 2025-06-15T10:12:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Endpoint tail behavior synthesis and multi-tenant SLO derivation

Tessa / team —

A couple of quick technical clarifications to add to the runbook before we hand it to Orion: 
- Sample at the replica level and then roll up; per-replica tail smoothing reduces noise from straggling hosts. For contractual evidence include both raw and smoothed percentiles.
- For safety we recommend capturing p999 and p9999 during the spike runs (sampled, not full retention) — these reveal rare tail modes we don't see in p99 alone.
- Prefix-cache warmup: recommend 45 minutes for our larger tenants (95th token length > 150) to avoid synthetic underestimation of cold-cache effects.
- For multi-tenant isolation tests, enforce CPU/GPU affinity and runtime cgroup limits so noisy neighbors are constrained; include pre/post host-level perf counters.

I'll update the workbook with these notes and add an appendix describing how we compute the headroom factor (statistical basis + operational safety margin).

Karthik
Principal Research Engineer, Redwood Inference
